summary.text: A biomolecule is a molecule produced by a living organism and essential to one or more biological processes.
The large ones are proteins, carbohydrates, lipids and nucleic acids, and small molecules such as vitamins and hormones count too.
Most biomolecules are organic compounds, and just four elements, oxygen, carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen, make up 96% of the human body's mass.

Big molecules count only when they are made inside the organism

items.prompt: A lab isolates a long polymer built from mononucleotides. It uses uracil instead of thymine, and its sugar rings carry an extra hydroxyl group. What is it?

options.label: DNA, built from deoxynucleotides
RNA, built from ribonucleotides
A polysaccharide, since it has sugar rings
A protein, since it is long and folds in 3D

items.explain: RNA uses the ribonucleotides C, G, A and U, which have an extra hydroxyl group on the pentose ring.

items.prompt: Two single sugars bond with removal of water, making a disaccharide. What is expected when it is boiled with dilute acid?

options.label: It joins with more sugars into a large starch
It turns into a single large nucleic acid
It stays unchanged because the bond is permanent
It splits back into its two single sugars

items.explain: Disaccharides can be hydrolyzed to yield their building blocks by boiling with dilute acid or reacting with enzymes.

items.prompt: Most RNA is thought of as a messenger carrying information. What else can some structured RNA molecules do?

options.label: Store genes as stable B-form double helices
Digest dietary proteins into amino acids
Act as enzymes that catalyse reactions
Serve only as a fuel for cellular respiration

items.explain: Structured RNAs can perform enzymatic catalysis, and are then known as ribozymes.

paragraphs.heading: Molecules made by life
paragraphs.text: A biomolecule, or biological molecule, is roughly any molecule a living thing makes that matters to one or more biological processes. The big ones are proteins, carbohydrates, lipids and nucleic acids; small ones such as vitamins and hormones count too. Many are endogenous, meaning the organism makes them itself, but living things usually also need some from outside, such as certain nutrients. Biology studies these molecules and their reactions, especially in biochemistry and molecular biology.

paragraphs.heading: A few elements do most of the work
paragraphs.text: Most biomolecules are organic compounds. Just four elements, oxygen, carbon, hydrogen and nitrogen, account for 96% of the mass of a human body. Many other elements, including various metals, are present in small amounts. Across the huge variety of life, the same kinds of biomolecules and the same chemical pathways keep turning up. Biologists call this sameness the biochemical universals, a unifying idea that stands beside cell theory and evolution.

paragraphs.heading: Nucleotides, the letters of DNA and RNA
paragraphs.text: A nucleoside forms when a nitrogen-containing base joins a ribose or deoxyribose sugar ring; adding phosphate groups to it gives a nucleotide. DNA and RNA are long chains, or polymers, built from these units by enzymes called polymerases. DNA uses the units C, G, A and T, while RNA uses C, G, A and U, whose sugar carries an extra OH group. Nucleotides also do other jobs: ATP and GTP store chemical energy, others carry signals inside the cell, and some are parts of helper molecules for enzymes.

paragraphs.heading: The shapes of DNA and RNA
paragraphs.text: DNA usually takes the shape of the double helix, held together by C pairing with G and A pairing with T. This pairing is precise and stable, and that is what lets DNA store genetic information reliably. RNA behaves differently: it can fold into large, complex 3D shapes that recall proteins, such as transfer RNA and ribosomes. Folded RNA can bind other molecules very specifically and can even speed up chemical reactions, in which case it is called a ribozyme.

paragraphs.heading: Sugars, from one to many
paragraphs.text: Carbohydrates come in sizes. Monosaccharides are the simplest, a single sugar such as glucose, fructose, galactose or ribose. Two of them joined, with water given off, make a disaccharide such as sucrose, maltose or lactose. Many joined together make a polysaccharide such as starch, cellulose or glycogen, usually large and often branched, while short chains of 3 to 10 units are called oligosaccharides. In the end most of these sugars serve as fuel for cellular respiration.

paragraphs.heading: Same sugar, different fates
paragraphs.text: Fructose and glucose leave the stomach at different speeds, are absorbed differently and are used differently afterwards. That gives the two sugars several separate routes to influence how much food we take in. Large polysaccharides do not dissolve in water because of their size, yet some form thick mixtures when heated in water.
